item.title: Tikoduadua: Let 9/11’s pain strengthen our commitment to peace
item.description: The September 11 attacks changed the face of global security forever, but Fiji must use the painful memory of the tragedy to strengthen its commitment to peace, Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said. Speaking at the United States Embassy in Suva today, during a commemoration marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks, Mr Tikoduadua said the world was never the same after 9/11.
item.content:encoded:
The September 11 attacks changed the face of global security forever, but Fiji must use the painful memory of the tragedy to strengthen its commitment to peace, Defence Minister Pio Tikoduadua said.

Speaking at the United States Embassy in Suva today, during a commemoration marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks, Mr Tikoduadua said the world was never the same after 9/11.

“The world was never the same after 9/11, and so many things have happened,” he said.

“But I think it’s also, while it is painful, it should also, you know, strengthen our conviction, to always make sure to work for peace, to live in peace.”

“That is what the world deserves, and our children deserve that.”

Acting Deputy Chief of Mission Somer Bessire-Briers said the ceremony honoured the 2,977 lives lost and those who responded to the attacks.

“On this solemn anniversary, we pause to honor the 2,977 innocent lives lost across New York, Virginia, and Pennsylvania,” she said.

“After September 11, people reached across borders, languages, religions, and cultures to say something very simple: We are with you. You are not alone.”

Acting Defence Attaché Major Clayton Shive said the victims came from more than 90 nations.

“On September 11, 2001, it wasn’t only Americans that lost their lives in the attack on the twin towers,” he said.

“Among the lost were citizens of more than 90 nations – a solemn reminder that it was not an attack on one country alone, but an attack on the shared futures and shared values of free people everywhere.”

The attacks involved four hijacked aircraft, two of which struck New York’s Twin Towers, while another hit the Pentagon and a fourth crashed in Pennsylvania.

Twenty-five years later, victims are remembered at Ground Zero, where their names are etched around reflecting pools marking the former towers.

The annual Tribute in Light, twin blue beams above lower Manhattan, has become a symbol of remembrance and resilience.

item.title: Two years suspended sentence for village hall arson
item.description: The High Court in Suva has handed down a two-year suspended prison sentence to 19-year-old Sairusi Rokosalu following his conviction for arson Justice Daniel Goundar delivered the ruling today, ordering that the two-year term be wholly suspended for three years.
item.content:encoded:
The High Court in Suva has handed down a two-year suspended prison sentence to 19-year-old Sairusi Rokosalu following his conviction for arson

Justice Daniel Goundar delivered the ruling today, ordering that the two-year term be wholly suspended for three years.

The court heard that on February 16, at approximately midday, Rokosalu intentionally set fire to old curtains inside the Nakorovatu Village Hall in Vunidawa using a gas lighter.

A fellow villager, Kamineli Ratova, spotted Rokosalu near the building shortly before black smoke was seen coming from the hall. Quick intervention by village youths, who poured water onto the building, contained the fire and prevented the total destruction of the communal facility, though material damage was caused to the hall and its contents.

The court heard the fire caused $13,350.50 in damage to the hall and its contents.

Rokosalu entered an early and unequivocal guilty plea, had no prior criminal record, and spent over three months deprived of liberty in remand custody and at Saint Giles Hospital for psychiatric evaluation.

Most significantly, medical reports and oral evidence from his father, Senitiki Naurisau, established that Rokosalu underwent neurological surgery as a young child. This left him with slow cognitive development, reading difficulties, and ongoing epilepsy.

The court determined that while his legal responsibility remained, these severe neurological and developmental impairments materially reduced his moral culpability, requiring a treatment-focused approach rather than immediate incarceration.

In suspending the sentence, Justice Goundar highlighted that Rokosalu’s family could provide a stable, supervised environment in the village to maintain his treatment, medication, and care. Traditional reconciliation had also been accepted by village leadership.

However, the judge cautioned that the suspension is a final opportunity rather than an act of indulgence, warning Rokosalu that any reoffending or breach of conditions within the three-year period will trigger the immediate execution of the prison sentence.

item.title: Sacred Hindu books damaged in temple break-in
item.description: Sacred religious books and other materials have allegedly been damaged or taken during a break-in at the Gopal Sadhu Hanuman Gadhi Mandir. The temple, in a social media post, said the alleged break-in occurred last night and also resulted in damage to temple property.
item.content:encoded:
Sacred religious books and other materials have allegedly been damaged or taken during a break-in at the Gopal Sadhu Hanuman Gadhi Mandir.

The temple, in a social media post, said the alleged break-in occurred last night and also resulted in damage to temple property.

“With great sadness and concern, we wish to inform our community that Gopal Sadhu Hanuman Gadhi Mandir was broken into last night,” the temple said.

It described the damage and loss of sacred religious books and materials as particularly distressing, saying they held deep spiritual, cultural and religious significance for the community.

The temple strongly condemned the incident and called on authorities to conduct a thorough investigation.

It has also called for CCTV footage and other available evidence to be examined and for increased police patrols and security around the temple and surrounding community.

“We urgently need stronger policing and increased security around our temple and surrounding community to prevent such incidents from happening again,” the statement said.

The temple has appealed to anyone who saw or heard anything unusual in the area last night, or who may have relevant CCTV or security footage, to contact Police or the temple committee.

“Our temple is a place of worship, peace and community. It must be protected and respected,” it said.

Community members have been urged to remain calm, united and vigilant while allowing authorities to investigate the incident.

item.title: High Court to review magistrate’s community treatment order powers
item.description: THE High Court in Suva has initiated a review into whether the law permits a magistrate to issue community-based treatment orders under the Mental Health Act based on medical recommendations. The matter involving Samuela Tawase was called today before Justice Daniel Goundar for first call.
item.content:encoded:
THE High Court in Suva has initiated a review into whether the law permits a magistrate to issue community-based treatment orders under the Mental Health Act based on medical recommendations.

The matter involving Samuela Tawase was called today before Justice Daniel Goundar for first call.

Justice Goundar directed both the prosecution and defence to file written submissions regarding a magistrate’s powers to impose such treatment orders.

Tawase, who was accused of attacking the Samabula Shiv Temple in July last year, was acquitted in May after the court found he was of unsound mind at the time of the offending.

Following his acquittal, Magistrate Yogesh Prasad released Tawase into the community under a compulsory community treatment order. The order followed expert testimony from a Saint Giles Hospital doctor who outlined Tawase’s ongoing mental health needs.

The court had heard that Tawase requires nightly medication and monthly injections to manage his condition, with doctors warning of a high risk of relapse and potential reoffending if he resumes substance abuse or defaults on his treatment.

Under the terms set by the Magistrates Court, Tawase was placed under family supervision to ensure compliance with his monthly clinical reviews, nightly medication, and a strict ban on alcohol and illicit drugs, including marijuana.

Magistrate Prasad had noted that the compulsory community treatment was intended to facilitate Tawase’s rehabilitation in the community while maintaining strict medical and family oversight.

Justice Goundar will hear the case on September 21.

item.title: ‘Leadership starts with discipline’
item.description: Being on time is more than simply being punctual – it demonstrates the respect, reliability and professionalism expected of a good leader, says Pacific Island Beverages director and co-founder Rajesh Patel. He shared this leadership lesson during the Leaders Lounge event, ‘Voices of Leadership’, held as part of Leadership Fiji’s 25th Anniversary celebrations.
item.content:encoded:
Being on time is more than simply being punctual – it demonstrates the respect, reliability and professionalism expected of a good leader, says Pacific Island Beverages director and co-founder Rajesh Patel.

He shared this leadership lesson during the Leaders Lounge event, ‘Voices of Leadership’, held as part of Leadership Fiji’s 25th Anniversary celebrations.

Mr Patel said his leadership perspective was shaped by 28-and-a-half years in the family business before leaving the Motibhai Group in 2022 to pursue entrepreneurship.

His career at the group spanned manufacturing, fast-moving consumer goods, importation, distribution, export, retail, print media, including The Fiji Times, and property management.

After a four-month break, he entered the ready-to-drink market and established Pacific Island Beverages in November 2022.

The company launched its first products in October 2023 with four alcoholic beverages and has since expanded to 23 products across alcoholic and non-alcoholic categories.

Mr Patel identified six key leadership lessons from his experience – discipline, self-awareness, relationships, investing in people, networking and giving back.

He said building strong and engaged teams was critical to organisational success.

“The most successful organisations are built by engaged people,” he said.

Mr Patel also urged emerging leaders to remain adaptable as technology, consumer expectations and workplaces continue to change.

“Today’s leaders must be adaptable, willing to learn and comfortable with change.”

He said entrepreneurship had taught him to embrace uncertainty and remain humble when making decisions.

“Entrepreneurship forces you to leave behind certainty and embrace ambiguity.

“It teaches you humility because each decision matters.”

item.title: FICAC officer takes stand
item.description: A FICAC investigating officer has agreed that two undisclosed witness statements would have been “helpful to the defence” of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad. Testifying during a voir dire proceeding before Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, Asenaca Niumataiwalu confirmed that statements from National Federation Party (NFP) officials, Kamal Iyer and Dalip Kumar were excluded from the pro
item.content:encoded:
A FICAC investigating officer has agreed that two undisclosed witness statements would have been “helpful to the defence” of former deputy prime minister Professor Biman Prasad.

Testifying during a voir dire proceeding before Magistrate Yogesh Prasad, Asenaca Niumataiwalu confirmed that statements from National Federation Party (NFP) officials, Kamal Iyer and Dalip Kumar were excluded from the prosecution’s disclosure.

Prof Prasad faces charges of failing to comply with statutory disclosure requirements and providing false information in a statutory declaration regarding Platinum Hotels and Resorts Pte Ltd.

Ms Niumataiwalu yesterday explained that she previously investigated Prof Prasad under file FEP 41 of 24 concerning a declaration for Lotus Construction, recording statements from Fijian Elections Office officer Mesake Dawai, NFP’s Tupou Draunidalo, Mr Iyer, and Mr Kumar.

She then recommended excluding Mr Iyer and Mr Kumar as unreliable witnesses to her superiors after a September 3, 2024, search warrant execution where both men allegedly withheld information and used vulgar language. The initial probe closed in April of 2025, while the current investigation (FEP 89 of 25) ran from July to October 2025.

Ms Niumataiwalu confirmed transferring statements from Ms Draunidalo and Mr Dawai to the new file, stating their statements were sufficient to prove the elements of the charge, while leaving out Mr Iyer and Mr Kumar’s March 2025 statements as irrelevant.

The court heard Ms Draunidalo’s statement was signed in November 2025, after Prof Prasad was charged on October 23, 2025.

Under cross-examination by defence lawyer Ashish Nand, Ms Niumataiwalu acknowledged that both files had similar issues despite involving different companies, and agreed that the men’s statements would have assisted the defence.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | Ratu Sukuna holiday
item.description: Heavy rain and blustery weather marked the first Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna Holiday celebrations at Albert Park, Suva, The Fiji Times reported on June 2, 1992. It was the first public holiday declared to honour Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna (1888-1958), the most distinguished Fijian of his time.
item.content:encoded:
Heavy rain and blustery weather marked the first Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna Holiday celebrations at Albert Park, Suva, The Fiji Times reported on June 2, 1992.

It was the first public holiday declared to honour Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna (1888-1958), the most distinguished Fijian of his time.

The holiday was recommended to Cabinet by the Great Council of Chiefs in October 1991.

To mark the day, a fundraising and bazaar — in which Fiji’s 14 provinces and Rotuma took part — was held at Albert Park.

The wet conditions did not dampen the spirits of almost 2000 people and guests who turned up to take part in the event.

Rain continued to fall in buckets. Huge puddles of water formed around the rim of the park and almost everybody walked around barefoot.

Large colourful umbrellas dotted the ground in an arc as they watched the then Tui Vuda and Vice-President, Ratu Sir Josaia Tavaiqia, open the celebrations.

The Tui Vuda spoke in Fijian about Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna and why a holiday was set aside.

Ratu Sir Josaia talked about Ratu Sir Lala’s interest in education for Fijians.

He then gave $5000 to Ratu Sukuna Memorial School as his contribution to fundraising efforts, mounted for improvements of facilities at the school in Nabua, just outside Suva.

Despite continuing rain, female students from the school waded in ankle-deep water into the grounds and performed a lively seasea (women’s dance), bringing a big round of applause from the audience.

Rain or no rain, the students appeared to have loved every minute of their task to provide entertainment.

Boys from the school then performed in what was a well-rehearsed meke wesi or spear dance.

The crowd enjoyed the dance as evident from the clapping and cheering.

Former Minister of Indian Affairs Irene Narayan took a tray around to collect donations from the people.

The provinces gave $500 each as their contribution towards the fundraising.

Each of the provinces and the RSMS Parents and Teachers Association and ex-students had a bazaar stall, selling Fijian handicraft and food.

At Borron House, almost 1000 people of all races came to see where the great statesman lived most of his life.

Lady Liku, widow of Ratu Sir Lala, said she was glad to be alive to see a public holiday declared for her late husband.

“This is a very important day for Fiji,” she said.

She thanked the president, former prime minister, and the chiefs of Fiji for the day.

Lady Liku said the day would remind the children of Fiji about Ratu Sir Lala and his achievements.

item.title: Clear legacy debts | Businesses urged to use amnesty period to settle $8m in arrears
item.description: The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation (FCEF) is issuing an urgent call to action for default businesses to clear outstanding Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) contributions, warning the window to clear millions in legacy debt under the present amnesty program was fast approaching. With more than $8 million still outstanding, including $4.8m from active employers, the Federation has partnere
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation (FCEF) is issuing an urgent call to action for default businesses to clear outstanding Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF) contributions, warning the window to clear millions in legacy debt under the present amnesty program was fast approaching.

With more than $8 million still outstanding, including $4.8m from active employers, the Federation has partnered with the FNPF to launch a nationwide series of divisional employer forums to help businesses resolve their debts amicably.

“I urge these employers to contact the FNPF urgently to resolve their cases amicably and before the end of the amnesty period,” FCEF chief executive officer Edward Bernard said.

Mr Bernard said the employer forum started with the Central Division on Tuesday this week.

“The objective is to reach out directly to employers through FCEF and resolve as many cases as possible.”

Mr Bernard said it was encouraging to see some employers had responded positively to the amnesty program, citing the recovery of $913,000, adding to the $2.8m recovered against the legacy debt of $10.8m.

“Social security is an important part of decent work and in the current labour market, aspiring to be a responsible and employer of choice is critical.

“Therefore, ensuring that statutory contributions are paid on time is also a strategy to attract and retain workers,” Mr Bernard said.

The Fund had also revealed that 1292 inactive employers owe $5.99m in legacy contribution debt.

Some debts date back to 1995 and includes complex cases involving businesses that had ceased operations, been liquidated or were being subjected to winding-up proceedings. While those debts were largely considered unrecoverable in those circumstances, the Fund continues to take appropriate recovery action wherever possible.

At the commencement of the amnesty campaign, the Fund had identified 2446 employers with legacy contribution debt, and 35,200 affected Fund members it intended to assist during the amnesty period.
